label: thm:A
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:A}
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every $P\in A(\overline K)$ the limit
\[
\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}(P)=\lim_{j\to\infty}4^{-j}h_{\boldsymbol w}\bigl(f([2^j]P)\bigr)
\]
exists. The function $\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}$ is a quadratic form, and there is a homomorphism $\ell_f\colon A(\overline K)\to\mathbf R$ such that
\[
h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))=\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}(P)+\ell_f(P)+O(1)\qquad(P\in A(\overline K)).
\]
\item If $f$ is finite, then $\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}$ is nonnegative and vanishes exactly on torsion points, and the number of points of a finitely generated subgroup $\Gamma\subseteq A(K)$ of rank $r\ge1$ with $h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))\le X$ is $c_\Gamma X^{r/2}+O(X^{(r-1)/2})$ with an explicit $c_\Gamma>0$.
\item Suppose that $f\circ[-1]=\bar\varphi\circ f$, where $\bar\varphi$ is the automorphism of $\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)$ induced by a graded automorphism $\varphi$ of the weighted polynomial ring. Then $\ell_f=0$ and $h_{\boldsymbol w}\circ f=\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}+O(1)$.
\end{enumerate}

label: thm:D
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:D}
Let $B$ be a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over a number field and $\beta\colon B\to\mathbf P^2$ a nonconstant morphism whose image contains $e$. Let $d_\beta=\deg\beta^*\mathcal O(1)$. Then the Jacobian family over $B$ has trivial trace, and there is $\delta_\beta>0$ such that, with $s_\beta=\delta_\beta/(2d_\beta)$,
\[
\widehat h_{J_b}(\sigma(\beta(b)))=s_\beta\,h_{\mathrm{inv}}(\beta(b))+O\bigl(\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{inv}}(\beta(b))+1}\bigr)
\]
for all $b\in B(\overline{\mathbf Q})$ whose fibre is smooth with $a\ne0$, where $h_{\mathrm{inv}}(\beta(b))$ is the weighted moduli height of that fibre. If $B$ has genus zero, the error term is $O(1)$. The slope $s_\beta$ depends only on the image curve $\beta(B)$. For each $n\ge1$ only finitely many $b\in B(\overline{\mathbf Q})$ of degree at most $n$ have $\sigma(\beta(b))$ torsion.

label: prop:monomial
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:monomial}
For every $x\in\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)(\overline K)$ one has $h(\nu_m(x))=m\,h_{\boldsymbol w}(x)$, and $\nu_m^*\mathcal O(1)\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)}(m)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Put $R_v=\max_i|x_i|_v^{1/w_i}$. For $\alpha\in\mathcal I_m$ we have $|x^\alpha|_v\le\prod_iR_v^{w_i\alpha_i}=R_v^m$, with equality for the pure power $x_j^{m/w_j}$ of an index $j$ realizing the maximum. Hence $\max_\alpha|x^\alpha|_v=R_v^m$ at every place, and summing gives the identity of heights. The second statement holds because $\nu_m$ is given by generating sections of the invertible sheaf $\mathcal O(m)$.

title: Proof
body_md: By Proposition~\ref{prop:monomial} the left side equals $h(\nu_m(f(P)))$, and $(\nu_m\circ f)^*\mathcal O(1)\simeq N$.

label: lem:eigen
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:eigen}
Let $S\in\operatorname{Pic}(A)\otimes\mathbf Q$ be symmetric and $M\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(A)\otimes\mathbf Q$. There are functions $\widehat h_S$ and $\lambda_M$ on $A(\overline K)$, with $\widehat h_S$ a quadratic form and $\lambda_M$ a homomorphism, such that $h_S=\widehat h_S+O(1)$ and $h_M=\lambda_M+O(1)$. Thus $\widehat h_S([n]P)=n^2\widehat h_S(P)$ and $\lambda_M([n]P)=n\lambda_M(P)$ for all $n\in\mathbf Z$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By the theorem of the cube, $[2]^*S\simeq S^{\otimes4}$ and $[2]^*M\simeq M^{\otimes2}$ \cite[Sections~6 and~8]{MumfordAV}. Hence $h_S([2]P)=4h_S(P)+O(1)$ and $h_M([2]P)=2h_M(P)+O(1)$, and Tate's telescoping argument shows that $\widehat h_S=\lim4^{-j}h_S\circ[2^j]$ and $\lambda_M=\lim2^{-j}h_M\circ[2^j]$ exist and differ from $h_S$, $h_M$ by bounded functions. The theorem of the cube gives the parallelogram law for $\widehat h_S$. For $M$, the addition map $\mu$ satisfies $\mu^*M\simeq p_1^*M\otimes p_2^*M$, so $h_M(P+Q)=h_M(P)+h_M(Q)+O(1)$; applying this to $([2^j]P,[2^j]Q)$ and dividing by $2^j$ shows that $\lambda_M$ is additive \cite{BombieriGubler,HindrySilverman}.

title: Proof

Applying it at $[n]P$ and using the scaling properties gives the second statement, and adding or subtracting the formulas for $P$ and $-P$ gives \eqref{eq:evenodd}.

label: ex:linear
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:linear}
The linear term is genuinely present in general. Let $E/K$ be an elliptic curve, $R\in E(K)$ a point of infinite order and $f_R\colon E\to\mathbf P^1$, $Q\mapsto x(Q-R)$. Then $f_R^*\mathcal O(1)\simeq\mathcal O_E(2(R))$, and the canonical height of the $x$-coordinate gives
\[
h(f_R(Q))=2\widehat h_E(Q-R)+O(1)=2\widehat h_E(Q)-4\langle Q,R\rangle_E+O_R(1).
\]
For $Q=[n]R$ this is $2n^2\widehat h_E(R)-4n\widehat h_E(R)+O(1)$, which differs from the quadratic term by an unbounded amount. The bundle $f_R^*\mathcal O(1)$ is ample but not symmetric.

label: def:wnt
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:wnt}
Let $f\colon A\to\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)$ be a morphism. The \emph{weighted N\'eron--Tate height} of $f$ is
\[
\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}(P)=\lim_{j\to\infty}4^{-j}\,h_{\boldsymbol w}\bigl(f([2^j]P)\bigr),\qquad P\in A(\overline K).
\]
head: environment

label: thm:wnt
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:decomposition} with $n=2^j$ and divide by $m4^j$: the linear term contributes $2^{-j}\ell_N(P)/m$ and the error is $O(4^{-j})$. This proves \eqref{eq:wnt}; replacing $m$ by $km$ replaces $N$ by $N^{\otimes k}$ and leaves $\frac1m\widehat h_{N^+}$ unchanged. If $f$ is finite, $N$ is ample because $\mathcal O(m)$ is ample on $\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)$, and then $N^+=\frac12(N+[-1]^*N)$ is ample; the last assertion is the classical property of N\'eron--Tate heights of ample symmetric classes.

label: thm:symmetric
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:symmetric}
Suppose that there is a graded $K$-algebra automorphism $\varphi$ of $K[X_0,\ldots,X_N]$ such that the induced automorphism $\bar\varphi$ of $\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)$ satisfies $f\circ[-1]=\bar\varphi\circ f$. Then $\ell_N=0$ and
\[
h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))=\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}(P)+O(1)\qquad(P\in A(\overline K)).
\]
If $\varphi$ is diagonal, $X_i\mapsto\varepsilon_iX_i$ with roots of unity $\varepsilon_i$, then $h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(-P))=h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))$ exactly.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Write $\varphi(X_i)=\varphi_i(X)$ with $\varphi_i$ weighted homogeneous of degree $w_i$. At every place, $|\varphi_i(x)|_v^{1/w_i}\le c_v\max_j|x_j|_v^{1/w_j}$ with $c_v=1$ for almost all $v$, and the same holds for $\varphi^{-1}$. Hence $h_{\boldsymbol w}(\bar\varphi(y))=h_{\boldsymbol w}(y)+O(1)$ on $\mathbf P(\boldsymbol w)(\overline K)$, and therefore $h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(-P))=h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))+O(1)$. By \eqref{eq:evenodd}, $\ell_N(P)=O(1)$ uniformly in $P$. Since $\ell_N([n]P)=n\ell_N(P)$ is bounded in $n$, we get $\ell_N=0$. For diagonal $\varphi$ the local maxima in \eqref{eq:hw} are unchanged.

label: cor:para
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:para}
If $f$ satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetric}, then
\[
\bigl|h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P+Q))+h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P-Q))-2h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))-2h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(Q))\bigr|\le C
\]
for a constant $C$ and all $P,Q\in A(\overline K)$. For arbitrary $f$ the same holds for the even height $\frac12\bigl(h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))+h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(-P))\bigr)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Both functions differ by a bounded amount from the quadratic form $\widehat h_{f,\boldsymbol w}$, by Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetric} and \eqref{eq:evenodd} respectively.

label: thm:count
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Write $P=T_0+\sum n_iP_i$ with $T_0\in T$ and $n\in\mathbf Z^r$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:wnt}, $h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))=n^tG_\Gamma n+b^tn+O(1)$ for some $b\in\mathbf R^r$, uniformly in $P$; both the quadratic and the linear part vanish on torsion. Completing the square, the condition $h_{\boldsymbol w}(f(P))\le X$ is sandwiched between $(n+c)^tG_\Gamma(n+c)\le X\mp C_1$ with $c=\frac12G_\Gamma^{-1}b$. The matrix $G_\Gamma$ is positive definite by Theorem~\ref{thm:wnt}. A translated ellipsoid of radius $\sqrt X$ contains $V_rX^{r/2}/\sqrt{\det G_\Gamma}+O(X^{(r-1)/2})$ lattice points, and multiplying by $|T|$ gives \eqref{eq:count}.

label: prop:metric
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:metric}
Let $\overline\mathcal H_1,\overline\mathcal H_2$ be two adelic metrics on a line bundle $\mathcal H$ on a projective variety $Y/K$, continuous at the archimedean places and equal at all but finitely many places. For $y\in Y(F)$ and a local section $s$ of $\mathcal H$ not vanishing at $y$,
\[
h_{\overline\mathcal H_2}(y)-h_{\overline\mathcal H_1}(y)=\frac1{[F:\mathbf Q]}\sum_{u\in M_F}n_u\log\frac{\|s(y)\|_{1,u}}{\|s(y)\|_{2,u}},
\]
and this difference is bounded on $Y(\overline K)$. In particular, for a morphism $f\colon A\to Y$ from an abelian variety, the limit of $4^{-j}h_{\overline\mathcal H}(f([2^j]P))$ does not depend on the adelic metric.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The local term is independent of $s$, since changing $s$ multiplies both norms by the same factor. At the finitely many places where the metrics differ, the ratio of the two norms is a continuous positive function on the compact analytic space $Y_u^{\rm an}$, hence bounded above and below.

label: thm:gitgeneral
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since the $I_i$ are $G$-invariant polynomials, $I_i(gy)=I_i(y)$ for all $g\in G(\overline K_v)$ and $y\in V(\overline K_v)$. At an archimedean place $|I_i(y)|_v\le\|I_i\|_1\|y\|_v^{w_i}$ by the triangle inequality, and at a finite place $|I_i(y)|_v\le\|y\|_v^{w_i}$ because $I_i$ has integer coefficients. Applying this to $y=gx$ and taking the infimum over $g$ proves (2). As $x$ is semistable, some $I_i(x)\ne0$, so $W_v(x)>0$ and $\rho_v(x)>0$ by (2); taking $g=1$ gives $\rho_v(x)\le\|x\|_v$. For all but finitely many $v$ the vector $x$ is primitive at $v$ and a fixed nonzero $I_i(x)$ is a unit, so $1=W_v(x)\le\rho_v(x)\le\|x\|_v=1$. Independence of $K$ holds because $\rho_v$ depends only on the place of $\overline K$; invariance under $G(\overline{\mathbf Q})$ is clear, and invariance under scaling follows from $\rho_v(\lambda x)=|\lambda|_v\rho_v(x)$ and the product formula. This proves (1). Summing (2) over all places, with $\sum_{v\mid\infty}n_v=[K:\mathbf Q]$, gives (3). For (4), $\rho_v(x)=\rho_v(gx)\le\|gx\|_v$ for every place. Finally (5) follows from (2) and $\rho_v(x)\le1$.

label: rem:reverse
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:reverse}
The inequality in (3) is effective. By Zhang's geometric reductivity at the archimedean places \cite{Zhang1994} and Burnol's results at the finite places \cite{Burnol}, the orbit-minimal norms define an adelic metric on $\mathcal O_Y(m)$, so that $h_{\mathrm{GIT}}-h_I$ is bounded on the semistable locus; see also \cite{Zhang1996}. The upper bound for $h_{\mathrm{GIT}}-h_I$ obtained in this way is not explicit, and only the effective inequality (3) is used below. Replacing the maximum norm by another norm at finitely many places changes $h_{\mathrm{GIT}}$ by a bounded amount. Zhang's normalized height of semistable cycles uses the Chow line and a normalization involving degree and dimension \cite{Zhang1996,ShaskaShaska}; to compare it with $h_I$ one has to identify the two metrized line bundles on $Y$, after which Proposition~\ref{prop:metric} applies.

label: prop:ICnorms
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:ICnorms}
The invariants $I_2,I_4,I_6,I_{10}$ are polynomials with integer coefficients in $a_0,\ldots,a_6$, with $4$, $16$, $56$ and $246$ monomials and
\[
\|I_2\|_1=302,\quad\|I_4\|_1=4192,\quad\|I_6\|_1=283842,\quad\|I_{10}\|_1=1561993.
\]
Their common zero locus in $\operatorname{Sym}^6$ over $\overline{\mathbf Q}$ is the set of sextics with a root of multiplicity at least four.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The first part is a direct expansion of \eqref{eq:IC}. The even-degree invariant ring of binary sextics in characteristic zero is generated by $I_2,I_4,I_6,I_{10}$, and the square of the odd invariant $I_{15}$ is a polynomial in them without constant term \cite{Igusa,Ottaviani}. Hence the four invariants vanish simultaneously exactly on the nullcone, which for sextics consists of the forms with a root of multiplicity at least four \cite{MumfordGIT}.

title: Proof
body_md: By Proposition~\ref{prop:ICnorms} we may apply Theorem~\ref{thm:gitgeneral}, with $c(I)=\max\{\frac12\log302,\frac14\log4192,\frac16\log283842,\frac1{10}\log1561993\}=\frac12\log302$. This gives (1) and (3) for $g\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\overline{\mathbf Q})$; for $g\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\overline{\mathbf Q})$ write $g=\lambda g_1$ with $g_1\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\overline{\mathbf Q})$, so that $gF=\lambda^6g_1F$ has the same projective height. For (2), if $F$ is primitive at $v$ and has good reduction there, then $I_{10}(F)=\operatorname{Disc}(F)$ is a $v$-adic unit and Theorem~\ref{thm:gitgeneral}(5) applies.

label: thm:local
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: At a prime $p$ the local weighted norm is $\max\{|Q_2|_p^{1/2},|D_5|_p^{1/5}\}$, whose logarithm is $\epsilon_p$; by Proposition~\ref{prop:pencil} it is $0$ for $p\notin\{2,3,5,7\}$. For $p=2$, $Q_2\equiv U^2\pmod2$, so a correction requires $U$ even and $T$ odd; then $v_2(D_5)=v_2(U)$, while $v_2(Q_2)=3$ if $v_2(U)=1$ and $v_2(Q_2)=2$ if $v_2(U)\ge2$, so the minimum is at most $1$, with equality when $v_2(U)\ge5$. For $p=3$, $Q_2\equiv T^2\pmod3$ forces $3\mid T$, $3\nmid U$, and then $v_3(Q_2)=1$. For $p=5$ the common zeros modulo $5$ are $T\equiv0$ and $T\equiv3U$, and for $p=7$ they are $T\equiv U$ and $T\equiv2U$. If $a$ is the relevant root and $v_p(T-aU)=1$ then $v_p(D_5)=1$; if $v_p(T-aU)\ge2$ then $Q_2\equiv Q_2(a,1)U^2\pmod{p^2}$ with $Q_2(a,1)\in\{15,7\}$ of valuation one. At the real place $Q_2=(2T-3U)^2+6U^2$; on the square $\max\{|T|,|U|\}=1$ its minimum is $\frac85$, at $(1,\frac25)$, and its maximum is $31$, while $|D_5|\le24$ and $24^{1/5}<\sqrt{31}$.

label: thm:surface
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:surface}
There is a nonempty Zariski-open subset $\mathcal U$ of $H^0(A,L)^{\oplus7}\simeq\mathbf A^{63}_\mathbf Q$ with the following property. For $\boldsymbol s=(s_0,\ldots,s_6)\in\mathcal U(\mathbf Q)$ every sextic $F_R=\sum_js_j(R)X^{6-j}Z^j$ with $R\in A$ is semistable, the general one is smooth, and the moduli morphism $\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}\colon A\to\mathcal X$ is finite onto a surface with $\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}^*\mathcal H\simeq L^{\otimes60}$. Moreover
\[
h_{\mathrm{inv}}(\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}(R))=3\widehat h_E(p_1R)+3\widehat h_E(p_2R)+O_{\boldsymbol s}(1).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $W=H^0(A,L)^{\oplus7}$. As $L$ is globally generated, evaluation at any $R$ is surjective onto $L_R^{\oplus7}$, so the tuples whose sextic at $R$ is unstable or zero form a subset of codimension three by Lemma~\ref{lem:codim}. The incidence variety of pairs $(R,\boldsymbol s)$ with $F_R$ unstable or zero has dimension at most $63+2-3=62$, so its image in $W$ is a proper closed subset. The tuples with $\operatorname{Disc}(F_{R_0})\ne0$ for a fixed $R_0$ form a nonempty open set, and $\mathcal U$ is the intersection; it has rational points because $\mathbf Q$ is infinite. For $\boldsymbol s\in\mathcal U$ the invariant $I_d(F_R)$ is a section of $L^{\otimes d}$, the invariant sections have no common zero, and the weighted monomials of degree $60$ identify $\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}^*\mathcal H$ with $L^{\otimes60}$. Ampleness of the pullback rules out contracted curves, so $\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}$ is finite. Since $L$ is symmetric, Theorem~\ref{thm:decomposition} has no linear term, and $h_{\mathrm{inv}}\circ\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}=\frac1{60}h_{L^{\otimes60}}+O(1)=h_L+O(1)$.

title: Proof
body_md: The main term comes from lattice points in the disks $3\widehat h_E(P_0)(n^2+m^2)\le X+O(1)$. The subgroups have rank at most one because $\Gamma$ is Zariski dense in $A$, since $P_0$ has infinite order, while $D_{\rm sing}$ is a curve. Since $\Phi_{\boldsymbol s}$ is finite, its geometric fibres have bounded cardinality.

title: Proof
body_md: Scale $(a,b,c)$ to be primitive at $v$; then the coefficient vector is primitive, since $a$, $b$ and $c$ all occur among its entries. title: Proof

title: Proof
body_md:
The six roots of $f_0$ are distinct modulo $13$ and $17$, so $C_0$ has good reduction there. Counting points gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
p&\#C_0(\mathbf F_p)&\#C_0(\mathbf F_{p^2})&\#J_0(\mathbf F_p)\\\hline
13&14&182&176=2^4\cdot11\\
17&18&286&288=2^5\cdot3^2
\end{array}
\]
Here, for a curve of genus two with $N_1$ points over $\mathbf F_p$ and $N_2$ points over $\mathbf F_{p^2}$, we put $c_1=N_1-p-1$ and $c_2=\frac12(c_1^2+N_2-p^2-1)$; the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius is $P_p(T)=T^4+c_1T^3+c_2T^2+pc_1T+p^2$ and $\#J(\mathbf F_p)=P_p(1)$. All Weierstrass points of $C_0$ remain rational and distinct modulo $13$, so $J_0(\mathbf F_{13})[2]$ has order $16$ and is the $2$-Sylow subgroup of $J_0(\mathbf F_{13})$. If the reduction of $D$ were killed by $2$, then $2P_\infty^+\sim2W$, and uniqueness of the hyperelliptic $g^1_2$ would force $P_\infty^+$ to be a Weierstrass point, which it is not. Hence $11$ divides the order of $D$ modulo $13$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:criteria}(1) with $\ell=11$, $p=13$, $q=17$ shows that $D$ has infinite order. A torsion section would specialize to a torsion class at $(O,O)$.

label: prop:trace
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:trace}
The generic fibre $\mathscr J_{\beta,\eta}$ has trivial $\mathcal K/\overline{\mathbf Q}$-trace, $\sigma_\beta$ has infinite order, and its N\'eron--Tate height $\delta_\beta=\widehat h_{\mathcal K}(\sigma_\beta)$ over $\mathcal K$, normalized by degrees on $B$, is positive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $b_0$ be a point over $e$. The fibre at $b_0$ is $(C_0,J_0)$ and $\sigma_\beta(b_0)=D$ has infinite order by Theorem~\ref{thm:nontorsion}, so $\sigma_\beta$ has infinite order. Let $(T,\tau)$ be the trace, with $\tau\colon T_{\mathcal K}\to\mathscr J_{\beta,\eta}$ of finite kernel. By Poincar\'e reducibility there is $\pi\colon\mathscr J_{\beta,\eta}\to T_{\mathcal K}$ with $\pi\circ\tau=[n]$ for some $n\ge1$. By the N\'eron mapping property both maps extend over a neighbourhood of $b_0$, and the identity $\pi\circ\tau=[n]$ persists. At $b_0$ we obtain $\tau_{b_0}\colon T\to J_0$ with finite kernel, so $J_0$ contains an abelian subvariety isogenous to $T$. If $\dim T=1$, this contradicts Lemma~\ref{lem:simple31}. If $\dim T=2$, then $\tau$ is an isogeny whose kernel is a finite subgroup of the constant abelian variety $T_{\mathcal K}$, hence constant, so $\mathscr J_{\beta,\eta}$ is isomorphic to a constant abelian surface; its principal polarization is constant as well, because the N\'eron--Severi group of a constant abelian variety does not change under the extension $\mathcal K/\overline{\mathbf Q}$. By Torelli the curves $C_{\beta(b)}$ would then be isomorphic over $\overline{\mathcal K}$, and the moduli map $\psi_2\circ\beta$ would be constant. This is impossible, because $\psi_2$ is finite (Theorem~\ref{thm:quadratic}) and $\beta$ is nonconstant. Hence $T=0$. By the Lang--N\'eron theorem the N\'eron--Tate height over $\mathcal K$ is positive definite modulo torsion when the trace vanishes \cite{Lang}, so $\delta_\beta>0$.

u_ eta$ with $

For $(u,v)\ne(0,0)$ and $d\in\mathbf Z\setminus\{0\}$,
\[
\delta_{du,dv}=d^2\delta_{u,v},\quad R_{du,dv}=d\,R_{u,v},\quad\delta_{v,u}=\delta_{u,v},\quad R_{v,u}=R_{u,v}.
\]
Hence the slope $s(u:v)=\delta_{u,v}/(6(u^2+v^2))$ is a well-defined function on $\mathbf P^1(\mathbf Q)$ with $s(v:u)=s(u:v)$.

title: Proof
body_md: Since $\alpha_{du,dv}=\alpha_{u,v}\circ[d]$, the fibre over $T$ for $(du,dv)$ is the fibre over $[d]T$ for $(u,v)$, and $U_{du,dv}=[d]^{-1}U_{u,v}$. Thus $\widehat h_J(\sigma_{du,dv}(T))=\delta_{u,v}d^2\widehat h_E(T)+2\langle T,dR_{u,v}\rangle_E+O(1)$, and uniqueness in Theorem~\ref{thm:ray} gives the first two identities. Since $\phi\circ s=\phi$ and $\alpha_{v,u}=s\circ\alpha_{u,v}$, the families for $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$ coincide.

label: thm:canonical-identities
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:canonical-identities}
Let $(u,v)\ne(0,0)$ and let $T\in E(\overline{\mathbf Q})$ have infinite order. Then $[n]T\in U_{u,v}$ for all but finitely many $n$, and
\begin{align*}
\lim_{|n|\to\infty}\frac{\widehat h_J(\sigma_{u,v}([n]T))}{n^2}&=\delta_{u,v}\,\widehat h_E(T),\\
\lim_{|n|\to\infty}\frac{h_{\mathrm{inv}}(\Phi_2(\alpha_{u,v}([n]T)))}{n^2}&=\widehat h_{\Phi_2\circ\alpha_{u,v},\boldsymbol w}(T)=6(u^2+v^2)\,\widehat h_E(T),\\
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\widehat h_J(\sigma_{u,v}([n]T))-\widehat h_J(\sigma_{u,v}([-n]T))}{4n}&=\langle T,R_{u,v}\rangle_E.
\end{align*}
In particular
\[
\lim_{|n|\to\infty}\frac{\widehat h_J(\sigma_{u,v}([n]T))}{n^2}=s(u:v)\cdot\widehat h_{\Phi_2\circ\alpha_{u,v},\boldsymbol w}(T),
\]
so the slope is the ratio of the N\'eron--Tate height of the section to the weighted N\'eron--Tate height of the moduli map along the curve $\alpha_{u,v}(E)$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:git-ray}
For every curve $\beta$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:general} and every $b\in B^\circ(\overline{\mathbf Q})$,
\[
\widehat h_{\mathscr J_{\beta,b}}(\sigma_\beta(b))\le s_\beta\,h_{\mathrm{GIT}}\bigl(F^{(2)}_{\beta(b)}\bigr)+O_\beta\Bigl(\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{GIT}}\bigl(F^{(2)}_{\beta(b)}\bigr)+1}\Bigr),
\]
with error $O_\beta(1)$ when $B$ has genus zero. With Remark~\ref{rem:reverse}, the N\'eron--Tate height is in fact $s_\beta h_{\mathrm{GIT}}+O(\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{GIT}}+1})$.
